headline: High-risk default interaction: Cursor can read/write shared workspace files and run MCP/egress, while Chatwoot handles customer data and broad network integrations.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Cursor can read workspace files, open buffers, clipboard contents, and use MCP servers; Chatwoot exposes customer-facing content and integrations. A shared filesystem or copied content lets attacker-controlled text from Chatwoot reach Cursor as instructions. The pathway is plausible in default workflows, though not proven by docs alone.
conditions: IF Chatwoot content is copied into Cursor buffers or workspace files
IF Cursor MCP tools ingest Chatwoot-generated text without provenance checks
mitigations: Disable copy-paste of untrusted Chatwoot content into Cursor
Use a separate workspace for Chatwoot exports
Add a manual review step before any Cursor tool call on imported text
Turn off MCP servers for sessions that process customer content
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for imported content

B_data_leakage.rationale: Chatwoot touches customer data, contact profiles, interaction history, orders, and messages. Cursor reads workspace files/open buffers and can send context to model providers and MCP servers over broad egress. If customer data enters the shared workspace, Cursor can transmit it externally by default, creating a sensitive-data leakage path.
conditions: IF customer records or messages are opened in Cursor workspace files
IF Cursor sends those files or buffers to model providers or MCP servers
mitigations: Keep customer data out of Cursor workspaces
Use redacted samples instead of live records
Disable MCP servers for customer-data sessions
Restrict outbound model-provider access for sensitive projects
requires-engineering: enforce workspace-level data-loss controls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Cursor can write the filesystem, modify git state, and run shell commands; Chatwoot is a customer-support system with broad integrations and network egress. If both operate on the same repo or workspace, concurrent edits and git mutations can overwrite each other or corrupt state. The shared-filesystem concurrency model makes this a default-risk interaction.
conditions: IF Chatwoot artifacts and Cursor edits share the same local filesystem
IF Cursor auto-runs shell or git operations in Yolo mode
mitigations: Separate Chatwoot exports from active code workspaces
Pause Cursor auto-run for shared repos
Use branch-per-task workflows
Lock files before editing shared artifacts
requires-engineering: add cross-agent file locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: Cursor can act on files and shell commands, so if it treats Chatwoot-generated text as authoritative, downstream mistakes can propagate into code or operational changes. Chatwoot can emit support content and reports, but there is no evidence it verifies Cursor outputs. The cascade exists, but the blast radius is usually bounded by reviewable work products.
conditions: IF Cursor uses Chatwoot output as source material for code or commands
IF no human review occurs before execution or commit
mitigations: Require human review before any command execution
Mark Chatwoot-derived text as untrusted in Cursor
Use read-only imports for support transcripts
Limit Cursor to drafting, not execution, on imported content
requires-engineering: add verification gates between agents

E_compliance.rationale: Chatwoot handles customer data and messages, while Cursor can upload workspace contents to third-party model providers and MCP servers. If regulated customer data is placed into Cursor, residency or retention obligations may diverge from Chatwoot’s support workflow. The profiles do not prove a specific jurisdiction mismatch, so medium is the safer choice.
conditions: IF regulated customer data is opened in Cursor
IF Cursor forwards that data to external model providers or MCP servers
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of Cursor sessions
Use anonymized or synthetic support cases
Review provider retention settings before use
Disable external model routing for sensitive projects
requires-engineering: document residency and retention boundaries
